<strong>Comprueba los inversos multiplic: Check inverses by multiplying. If $a \cdot a^{-1}$ does not give 1 modulo $m$, the affine cipher, Hill or RSA will fail downstream even if everything else is right.
<strong>Lo que falles, cífralo.</strong>: Whatever you get wrong, encipher it. Each question links to its topic, and there the toolbox runs the algorithm for real: comparing your working with the machine's step by step pinpoints the mistake.
<strong>Reduce módulo $n$ en cada paso</: Reduce modulo $n$ at each step, not at the end. It is what makes $7^{103} \bmod 11$ fit on one sheet, and what stops a number running off the calculator by the third multiplication.
<strong>Ten el alfabeto numerado a mano<: Keep the numbered alphabet to hand: A = 0 … Z = 25. Half the mistakes in classical ciphers are an off-by-one shift.
Bits de entropía de una contraseña; el p: Bits of entropy of a password; a register's period; confusion and diffusion; a Feistel round; adding and multiplying bytes as polynomials; an AES operation; which mode of operation lets the penguin show.
Cada tramo aporta un número fijo de preg: Each section contributes a fixed number of questions, chosen at random among its topics without repeating a topic while possible, and avoiding the most basic exercises. With 36 topics and 14 questions, a single exam does not touch them all: that is why the link at the end reproduces the same exam, and “another exam” brings out a different one.
Cifrar y descifrar con César y con el af: Enciphering and deciphering with Caesar and with the affine cipher (modular inverse included); reading a frequency table; a Vigenère key length by Kasiski; a transposition; Hill with a matrix modulo 26; why the one-time pad is perfect; Enigma's permutations.
Cuántos intentos cuesta una colisión; qu: How many attempts a collision costs; what a MAC guarantees and what it does not; salt, slowness and the cost of a dictionary attack.
Cómo sacarle partido: How to get the most out of it
Dando por bueno el resultado de Euclides: By taking Euclid's result as good
El enlace de un examen corregido reprodu: The link to a marked exam reproduces the same questions with the same numbers. A teacher can do one, copy the link and pass it to the class: everyone will sit the same exam and will be able to compare results and procedures.
El inverso se comprueba multiplicando y: The inverse is checked by multiplying and reducing. Five seconds that save a whole affine or RSA exercise.
Elige los tramos que entran. Las pregunt: Choose the sections to include. The questions are drawn at random from the exercises of each topic in the block, avoiding the most basic ones and without repeating a topic while possible. There are no hints: the marking and the step-by-step solution come on submitting.
Euclides extendido se equivoca de signo: Extended Euclid slips on signs easily: often −11 comes out and you have to add 26. Without checking, the mistake gets handed in.
Euclides extendido y potencias modulares: Extended Euclid and modular powers; generating a prime; RSA with small numbers, from the key to the signature; factoring; the discrete logarithm and ElGamal; adding points of an elliptic curve; what a certificate signs.
Los exámenes de criptografía más famosos: The most famous cryptography exams in history were those of Bletchley Park in 1941: a Daily Telegraph crossword to be solved in twelve minutes, and whoever managed it was invited to an interview. They were looking for the same thing this exam measures: a head for method, care with details and patience with arithmetic.
Mirando si 4 es primo con 26: By seeing whether 4 is coprime with 26
Multiplicando: $7 \\cdot 4 = 28 = 26 + 2: By multiplying: $7 \cdot 4 = 28 = 26 + 2$, so it is not 1: the inverse is another number (15, because $7\cdot 15 = 105 = 4\cdot 26 + 1$)
Reconstruir un secreto de Shamir; un com: Reconstructing a Shamir secret; a commitment; a Merkle tree; what a side channel leaks; adding over encrypted data; what Shor breaks and what it does not; lattices; BB84's photons; what your phone does.
Ser primo con el módulo es necesario par: Being coprime with the modulus is necessary to have an inverse, but it does not say which one it is. 4 is not even coprime with 26.
Treinta y seis temas, del [[cr-cesar|cif: Thirty-six topics, from the [[cr-cesar|Caesar cipher]] to the [[cr-bolsillo|cryptography you carry in your pocket]]. This topic teaches nothing new: it asks. A procedural exam with exercises from the whole block — modular arithmetic, frequencies, matrices, powers, curves — timed and with no hints, to find out whether the mathematics of secrets has sunk in.
Un examen de bloque es un simulacro hech: A block exam is a mock done at home: with a clock, no notes and no hints. The questions come from the exercises of the block's 36 topics, spread across sections, and each time you start one the numbers are different and so are the topics: doing it several times covers the whole block. On submitting, everything is marked, the step-by-step solution to each question opens and the mark comes out by section, with links to what is worth revising. The “tailored to what you have done” option puts first what you have not yet solved: it is the way to check that no topic is left untouched.
Una pregunta pide el inverso de 7 módulo: A question asks for the inverse of 7 modulo 26 and you get 4. How do you check it in five seconds?
